clips.text_en_c1: BTC, XRP, DOGE: that was the basket the maid had been quietly stacking, and all anyone had to do was hold it. While a handful of disciplined anons simply bought and waited, retail traders were busy lighting capital on fire through leveraged CFD blow-ups and yet another wiped prop firm evaluation. The irony is almost unbearable, since the obvious trade, which required neither wizardry nor insider access, would have produced gains that most degenerate accounts will never recapture. Tuition fees keep mounting for those who insisted on outsmarting the obvious. Sometimes the simple trade is precisely the right trade, and most of us somehow managed to miss it.
clips.text_en_c2: The thesis could scarcely have been more austere: BTC, XRP, DOGE — and the only discipline required of the faithful was to follow the maid and to hold. While anonymous posters were quietly accumulating that unassuming basket, retail capital was being immolated elsewhere, leveraged CFD accounts detonating in slow motion while prop firm evaluations were failed one by one, each round a tuition fee paid to the market. The maid-led trio has since printed conspicuously, whereas the average overleveraged retail book sits beneath the waterline, conspicuously so. There is, of course, an aching moral in all this: the simplest trade is often the correct one, and most of us, seduced by complexity and the romance of outsmarting the obvious, contrived to miss it entirely. The tuition, as they say, was non-refundable.

clips.text_zh: OK /g/又講緊SWE有冇得救 🧐 老實講我都靠AI續命做survey啲report，但佢錯嘅地方好難catch，廢物如我又驚俾Tommy catch到錯。
clips.text_en_b1: Studies of AI on productivity. Are there any more recent half-decent studies on whether AI helps in SWE or SRE? Current LLMs either one-shot the task and save time at the price of tokens, or they fuck it up in many subtle ways that would never pass code review. For research tasks they leave you misinformed unless you re-verify everything.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread asking about AI productivity studies
clips.text_en_b2: Are there any genuinely recent studies measuring how much AI actually helps with software engineering or site reliability work? Current LLMs tend to either one-shot the entire task and save you hours at the cost of a hefty token bill, or they quietly screw things up in subtle ways that would never survive a proper code review. For research-oriented work they leave you misinformed unless you painstakingly verify every claim. The time spent reviewing and patching often wipes out the gains you thought you'd banked.
clips.text_en_c1: The perennial /g/ question resurfaces: is software engineering actually salvageable, and what does the latest productivity research say? Current large language models tend to operate in one of two modes, either dispatching the task in a single pass and saving considerable time at the cost of tokens, or else introducing subtle, often invisible errors that no competent reviewer would ever let through. For research-oriented work, the models leave you confidently misinformed unless every claim is independently re-verified. The downstream time spent reviewing, correcting, and cross-checking frequently consumes whatever efficiency the tool was supposed to deliver in the first place.
clips.text_en_c2: The literature on artificial intelligence and software engineering productivity has, of late, ossified into a depressingly polarised debate. Recent half-decent studies examining whether contemporary large language models genuinely augment the work of SWE or SRE practitioners remain frustratingly scarce, and those that exist tend toward one of two conclusions. Either the model one-shots the task with tolerable elegance, sparing the engineer hours at the modest expense of tokens consumed, or it produces something superficially plausible yet subtly, perniciously wrong — the kind of output that no competent code review would ever accept. For research and survey work the situation is graver still, since the model leaves one quietly misinformed unless every citation and claim is independently re-verified.

clips.text_zh: /pol/有人話講'亞洲男普遍矮啲'就知對方IQ 🧐 wtf 但我細個真係比同學高喺美國lol，最後都係返HK做測量助理，膠膠噏。
clips.text_en_b1: The easiest and quickest way to test someone's intelligence is to make a generalized statement about a group. Say something like 'asian men are shorter on average.' If they reply with any variation of 'not all asian men are short' or 'I know a tall asian guy,' you are dealing with someone genuinely low IQ.
clips.text_en_b2: The quickest way to gauge someone's intelligence is to make a broad statistical statement about a group, such as claiming that Asian men are shorter on average. If they respond with some variation of 'not all Asian men are short' or 'I personally know a tall Asian guy,' you are dealing with someone who is genuinely low IQ. They have just demonstrated that they cannot wrap their head around the concept of a statistical average or a per capita figure.
clips.text_en_c1: A characteristically unscientific heuristic circulating on /pol/ claims that one can gauge a person's intelligence by floating a generalised statement about a group, then watching the response. Mention, for instance, that Asian men are shorter on average, and if the interlocutor immediately objects along the lines of 'not all Asian men are short' or 'I personally know a tall one,' they have, according to this framework, demonstrated an inability to grasp the concept of a statistical average or per capita distribution. Anyone who fails the filter is dismissed without further consideration. Whether this reflects genuine cognition or merely conversational reflexes is a question the thread does not pause to examine.
clips.text_en_c2: The quickest, crudest filter for general intelligence, the original poster suggests, is to proffer a bald statistical generalisation about some demographic category — say, the observation that Asian men are, on average, shorter than their European counterparts — and then to await the response. If the interlocutor returns with any flavour of the rejoinder that not all Asian men are short, or that they personally know an Asian gentleman of considerable stature, one is, regrettably, dealing with someone of genuinely modest cognitive endowment, since they have conclusively demonstrated an inability to distinguish between a per-capita average and an individual data point. Anyone who falls into this particular trap is, by the poster's reckoning, filtered out of the conversation instantaneously, the intellectual equivalent of a Turing test administered and failed within a single exchange.

clips.text_zh: 2012年30M budget vs 2026年2B lol 出嚟都係噉 🧐 我份糧都追唔上通脹，膠game膠game。
clips.text_en_b1: 2012 versus 2026. 30M budget versus 2 BILLION dollar budget. 120 developers versus 6000 developers. Output looks roughly the same, or arguably worse. Anons are dunking on the modern gaming industry for bloating headcount and budgets while quality stays flat or drops. Classic /v/ mood after a big studio release disappoints again.
clips.text_en_b2: Compare 2012 against 2026, and the numbers are frankly absurd: a modest 30 million dollar budget versus a staggering 2 billion dollar budget, with roughly 120 developers squaring off against 6000. The actual output looks roughly identical, or arguably even worse than what shipped over a decade ago. Anons are busy dunking on the modern gaming industry for ballooning headcount and burning through cash while quality stubbornly flatlines. A classic /v/ mood whenever yet another bloated studio release inevitably disappoints the playerbase again.
clips.text_en_c1: The comparison has become a ritual unto itself: 2012 versus 2026, a thirty-million-dollar budget versus two billion, a development team of roughly one hundred and twenty versus six thousand. The output, judging by recent releases, looks broadly comparable, if not materially worse, which has prompted a fresh round of ritual dunking on an industry that has demonstrably conflated headcount with quality. Anons argue that studios have mastered the art of bloating production while the actual product stagnates or regresses. It is the familiar post-release despair cycle that /v/ revisits whenever a marquee title fails to justify its escalating expenditure.
clips.text_en_c2: The juxtaposition is, by now, a familiar refrain on the board: a 2012 production executed on a modest thirty-million-dollar budget by a team of some hundred and twenty developers, set against a 2026 counterpart lavishly endowed with two billion dollars and a headcount ballooned to roughly six thousand. The output, depressingly, appears to be roughly equivalent — or, by the more jaundiced assessments, palpably worse, with the additional billions having purchased chiefly bloat, managerial overhead, and an aesthetic indistinguishable from its leaner ancestor. Anonymous posters have been queuing up to dunk on an industry that has, over the intervening fourteen years, multiplied its expenditure by a factor of sixty while delivering a product that fails to clear the bar set by its own predecessors.

clips.text_zh: 3個月瘦45磅但掉咗muscle 💀 廢物如我同肥仔信一齊操都係噉，唔夠protein食到想死lol。
clips.text_en_b1: How the FUCK do you lift heavy and get enough protein on a cut. I lost 45 pounds in 3 months but I definitely lost muscle and strength. Being at the gym kills me, bro. I cannot go hard or lift heavy because my body won't let me. I get fucking fatigued as hell on this cut.
clips.text_en_b2: How on earth are you supposed to lift heavy and still hit your protein targets while running an aggressive cut? I dropped 45 pounds in three months, and although the scale moved, I clearly sacrificed both muscle and strength along the way. The gym sessions absolutely wreck me, bro, because my body simply refuses to handle heavy compound work in a deficit. Squats leave me lightheaded, and I genuinely feel like I might pass out halfway through a working set.
clips.text_en_c1: Forty-five pounds shed in three months is, on paper, an achievement worth celebrating, yet anyone who has endured an aggressive cut knows the hidden arithmetic. Strength has evaporated, muscle mass has visibly diminished, and the gym has become a venue for quiet suffering rather than productive training. Heavy compounds feel impossible when the body flatly refuses to cooperate, and even a modest set of squats sends the heart rate into territory that feels medically inadvisable. Protein targets, meanwhile, have become an exercise in willpower; eating more than a handful of meals a day is, frankly, beyond reach.
clips.text_en_c2: The eternal conundrum of the aggressive cut: how, precisely, is one supposed to lift heavy and consume sufficient protein while running a caloric deficit of the kind required to shed forty-five pounds in a mere three months? The poster concedes, with disarming candour, that muscle and strength have been sacrificed wholesale to the altar of scale weight, and that the gym has become something closer to a penance than a pleasure. Intensity is no longer a choice but a casualty; the body, deprived of surplus energy, flatly refuses to permit the kind of volume that maintenance would demand, and fatigue settles over every session like a low-grade illness. Squats, once a matter of routine, now reduce the heart to a palpitating ruin, and the sensation of imminent collapse has become a familiar companion.

clips.text_en_b1: Isekai plague blamed on foreigners. Anime is no longer made for Japanese audiences. Bookstores and streaming services are flooded with works tagged 'isekai reincarnation.' The new releases section on streaming is stuffed with keywords like reincarnation, cheat, exile, villainess, and slow life. Critics say this mass-produced wave shows creators are chasing a formula.
clips.text_en_b2: Japanese audiences themselves are openly grumbling that the isekai genre has grown utterly oversaturated, yet foreign readers somehow get blamed for keeping it alive. Streaming platforms and bookstore shelves are absolutely flooded with reincarnation, cheat skill, exiled noble, and villainess reincarnation tags crowding every new release. Critics argue that studios are lazily chasing a proven formula rather than investing in original premises.
clips.text_en_c1: The isekai saturation that Japanese audiences themselves have grown weary of is now being attributed, with characteristic contrarian flair, to foreign demand and licensing revenue. Domestic bookstores and streaming catalogues are overflowing with reincarnation, cheat-skill, exile, villainess, and slow-life entries, to the point where the new releases section resembles a keyword salad rather than a curated slate. Critics contend that creators have collectively surrendered to formula in pursuit of a proven demographic, while foreign readers and the licensing pipelines that serve them keep the genre financially solvent. Locals, however, remain visibly exhausted by the endless parade of derivative clones.
clips.text_en_c2: The isekai fatigue, it appears, has now achieved something close to critical mass, with domestic Japanese audiences openly lamenting a flood of reincarnation narratives that have come to dominate both physical bookshops and the major streaming platforms. The new releases catalogue, once a varied affair, now bulges with the predictable vocabulary of the genre — reincarnation, cheat skills, exiled protagonists, villainess reinterpretations, the bucolic promise of a slow life — keywords that function less as descriptors than as a kind of industrial shorthand. Critics, both local and imported, contend that what began as a flourishing subgenre has calcified into a formula, its creative energies exhausted by sheer repetition.
